text: Logan Finney July 17, 2020 Head: Owyhee County schools solidifying reopening plans Subhead: Possible mask requirements cause tension in region 933 words The Marsing school board approved reopening plans for their district last week, building upon the green, yellow and red framework released by the state with corresponding plans for traditional, hybrid and remote instruction. The Wednesday meeting featured a town hall period for officials to answer attendees’ questions and explain details. A representative from Southwest District Health also attended virtually to give feedback on the proposal. Marsing superintendent Norm Stewart said that although the 12-person crowd was a smaller turnout, there was plenty of input from the community. “There was some concern about not having masks and then there was concern about requiring kids to wear masks,” Stewart said in an interview Thursday. He said that under the plan, masks are recommended but not required. “We’ve already ordered masks for every staff member, and we are ordering masks for every student so that when everyone starts the school year everyone will at least have a mask.” After the town hall and SWDH’s help with some technical rewording, the board approved the document, which comes in both a plain language version for parents and students and a more formal version with resources for the district. “It really was a means to be able to improve and take what we’ve learned through the spring and improve,” Stewart said. “Whether we’re in session, whether we’re in rolling closures or extended closures.” “The teachers recognize that we need to treat that situation if we are in an extended period like the parents are almost substitute teachers. Just like we’d have to do a lesson plan for a sub, we need to do kind of a lesson plan to give a little bit more direction.” Case numbers have increased recently in Owyhee County, but Stewart said that today the district would hypothetically be open with traditional instruction at the low end of the “yellow” category under minimal to moderate community spread. “Our ultimate goal is to be in session and to have kids here and continue with face to face delivery if at all possible.” Bruneau-Grand View superintendent Ryan Cantrell is also preparing for an in-person opening in his district. “Our families have indicated a strong preference for face to face instruction in the fall,” Cantrell said. “The vast majority of what I’m hearing is ‘When are we opening? When are we coming back?’” The Bruneau-Grand View school board has seen a few versions of the district’s plan, Cantrell said, but they will continue to update the document until the board considers it at their regular August meeting. Their plan also recommends masks but does not require them, except in the particular case of a student who has a fever but has to ride the bus to the school and have family pick them up. Cantrell said in his remote and rural district, they may have issue on long bus routes if a child shows a fever, but their guardian has already left for work. “Our bus drivers have asked for touchless thermometers so they can scan kids as they get on the bus, which I’m great with,” Cantrell said. “How are we going to isolate them if they’re showing symptoms? Each school is really having to work on what are we going to do for a sick room or some kind of isolation room where that kid can hang out by themselves until there parent gets there. Being in a rural district, some of our parents are working 30 to 60 minutes away from our school.” The district has purchased 500 reusable cloth masks to offer teachers and students. “We’ll essentially have two five-gallon buckets. When you get on you’ve got a bucket for clean masks and when you get off you throw it in the dirty bucket, then we’ll wash and sanitize them and reuse them.” Both districts have plans for multiple sanitizing stations at school entrances and in classrooms. If COVID-19 cases increase dramatically, however, the mask decision may be taken out of their hands. “There were questions with Central District Health requiring Ada County to be in masks,” said Stewart. “What if Southwest District Health made that same requirement through their board meeting that was supposed to be today? Was that going to be Canyon County, or was that going to be Canyon and Owyhee County?” The SWDH board was supposed to meet via Zoom teleconference Thursday morning to hear from regional hospitals and consider future mitigation efforts, including a potential mask mandate. After delays, the meeting was cancelled. “Prior to the start of the Board meeting, a group of protesters gathered at the entrance to the SWDH Caldwell building demanding to physically attend the meeting in the same room as Board members,” the district said in a news release. Video posted to Facebook by one of the protestors that day shows Ammon Bundy shoving a staff member who was attempting to block him from entering the door. The Southwest District Health meeting will be rescheduled. Eastern Idaho Public Health recently implemented a mask mandate for Teton County and banned large gatherings there, the Post Register reports. “Where we’re a joint school district,” Stewart said, “part of our students come from Canyon County. We’re trying to understand how that [a mask requirement] would pertain to us as we bus and transport kids from Canyon County to our school district in Owyhee County.” “You know, do you have to wear a mask until you cross the river? What does that really look like?” he joked. “Those are some details that are still yet to be worked out depending on what decisions come from Southwest District Health.” ### NOTES NOTES NOTES NOTES NOTES NOTES NOTES NOTES Stewart: “Really it’s going to be about us trying to educate. Educate our staff and our kids on appropriate use of masks and sanitizing and personal hygiene in regard to this whole situation.” “We’ll try to intervene if there’s large groups congregating in areas. We may have to do some verbal correction as far as asking people to separate and provide more distance,” said Stewart. “The whole goal is not to play the mask police or to play the gotcha game, its more about trying to help kids –and adults for that matter—at least acknowledge and be aware of the fact that we do have a need to try to protect each other and try to put some distance between ourselves and others. That’s also really difficult when you have a group of elementary kids out on the playground.” Marsing distance learning If cases do increase enough to require tighter restrictions, plan is physical packets with tech enrichment for elementary school students, with a preference for seeing them every day. Middle school students blended learning with packets and online instruction. At the middle school students are assigned individual Chromebooks to use, which could be sent home if distance learning was needed. High school students are already assigned Chromebooks which they take class to class under the traditional model. More check-ins and interactions between staff and students. More effort into connecting with parents to make sure distance learning is implemented at home effectively. “Part of the issue that we ran into, especially at the elementary, was packets were being sent home but the parents not understanding either how much each student should do on each day, or how to even teach the student how to do the packet.” said Stewart. Bruneau, Grand View, Oreana “Our 6-12 school, which is Rimrock, only has 185 kids,” Cantrell said. “And in addition to that 185 low count, our bells are offset. We have a set of bells for six, seven, eight and then a separate set of bells for high school, so when we have our passing periods we’re only going to have 80 or 90 kids in the hallway at a time.” “The way our school is set up naturally, we’re pretty well set up to this just to start with.” “Of course, that can change in a real hurry as more people get tested, or it can just change as it passes through. But right now—last we heard—we were either at that low or moderate risk.” “We were very hesitant to close in the spring,” Cantrell said. “We were one of the last school districts to finally close it down in the spring, and that was honestly as much peer pressure as anything else. When you’ve got the liability of being the only district open or one of the few open, if something happens then you have a hard time clinging to that reasonable person standard and you start to increase your risk and liability when that happens.” Liability protections have been one topic Governor Little has cited as a potential reason to convene a special session of the legislature.
